title: Antimicrobial use guidelines for canine pyoderma by the International Society for Companion Animal Infectious Diseases (ISCAID)
citation: Loeffler A, et al. Vet Dermatol. 2025;36(3):234-282. doi:10.1111/vde.13342
evidence_type: Clinical guideline + systematic literature review + consensus
key_points: Cytology is central to diagnosis and antimicrobial decision-making.
Topical antimicrobial therapy is preferred where appropriate for surface/superficial pyoderma.
Systemic antimicrobials should be reserved for cases where topical therapy is insufficient or impractical, especially deep disease.
Underlying causes of recurrent pyoderma should be investigated.

title: Diagnosis and treatment of dermatophytosis in dogs and cats: Clinical Consensus Guidelines of the World Association for Veterinary Dermatology
citation: Moriello KA, et al. Vet Dermatol. 2017;28(3):266-e68. doi:10.1111/vde.12440
key_points: Diagnosis should integrate clinical findings with fungal testing rather than relying on lesion appearance alone.
Systemic and topical therapy are generally used together for generalized dermatophytosis.
Environmental decontamination is an important component of management.

title: Diagnosis and treatment of demodicosis in dogs and cats: Clinical consensus guidelines of the World Association for Veterinary Dermatology
citation: Mueller RS, et al. Vet Dermatol. 2020;31(1):5-27. doi:10.1111/vde.12806
evidence_type: Clinical consensus guideline with literature review
key_points: Deep skin scrapings are a diagnostic gold standard, with trichograms/tape-squeeze preparations useful in selected cases.
Isoxazolines have demonstrated good efficacy for canine demodicosis.
Adult-onset generalized demodicosis warrants evaluation for underlying immunosuppressive disease.

title: Canine atopic dermatitis: detailed guidelines for diagnosis and allergen identification
key_points: Canine atopic dermatitis is a clinical diagnosis requiring exclusion of mimicking/overlapping conditions.
Flea assessment, skin scraping and cytology are used as indicated in the work-up.
Elimination diet trials are required in appropriate perennial pruritus/concurrent GI cases before attributing signs solely to environmental allergy.

title: Treatment of canine atopic dermatitis: 2015 updated guidelines from the International Committee on Allergic Diseases of Animals (ICADA)
key_points: Acute flares require identification/removal of flare factors plus antipruritic/anti-inflammatory treatment.
Oclacitinib and glucocorticoids are among options for acute flare control.
Long-term management is multimodal and includes trigger control, skin care and evidence-supported anti-inflammatory therapy.

title: Clinical Guidelines for the Use of Antipruritic Drugs in the Control of the Most Frequent Pruritic Skin Diseases in Dogs
citation: Souza CP, et al. Animals (Basel). 2022;12(8):984. PMID:35448647
key_points: Evidence and recommendations differ by disease context; symptomatic antipruritic therapy should not replace etiologic work-up.
Glucocorticoids, ciclosporin, oclacitinib and lokivetmab have varying evidence-supported roles in common canine pruritic diseases.

title: A systematic review of allergen immunotherapy, a successful therapy for canine atopic dermatitis and feline atopic skin syndrome
citation: Mueller RS. J Am Vet Med Assoc. 2023;261(S1):S30-S35. doi:10.2460/javma.22.12.0576
key_points: Allergen immunotherapy is the disease-modifying treatment directed at relevant allergens after clinical diagnosis and allergen identification for treatment selection.

title: Oclacitinib 10 years later: lessons learned and directions for the future
citation: Marsella R, et al. J Am Vet Med Assoc. 2023;261(S1):S36-S47. doi:10.2460/javma.22.12.0570
key_points: Reviews a decade of efficacy and safety experience with oclacitinib for canine allergic/atopic dermatitis.
Off-label extrapolation to unrelated immune-mediated diseases should not be treated as equivalent evidence.
